video_title: What $450M Portfolio Manager Learned From Paul Tudor Jones  · Andrew Perry
gist: Ex-Tudor PM Andrew Perry (Macro Pillars) explains his five-pillar macro framework centered on policy and non-traditional liquidity, especially Treasury refunding duration (e.g., Nov 1, 2023) and key policy dates as price levels, plus why the MOVE index matters more than the VIX. He details recent trades (short KOSPI/Taiwan, long corn/wheat/soy on the Middle East crisis), bearishness on crypto lagging key dates, and Tudor-style risk discipline (55-57% win rates, hard stops, drawdown limits).

insights.claim: Andrew Perry's Macro Pillars framework has five parts: (1) government policy/geopolitics, (2) non-traditional liquidity (Treasury quarterly refunding duration, fiscal policy), (3) traditional monetary policy, (4-5) key dates/technicals and price response, with execution as the final step.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: A checklist for layering policy, liquidity, dates and price before sizing a macro trade.
insights.quote: pillar two is what I call non-traditional liquidity and that's the quant that's the quantitative refunding they do every quarter

insights.claim: Perry built the pillars after being run over short on March 20, 2020, when the Fed bought corporate credit and global central banks cut to zero, turning a COVID lockdown into a market 'casino' he had failed to anticipate.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Short theses based on economic damage fail when policy floods the system with liquidity; watch what policymakers do, not say.
insights.quote: Now I was still trading short and got completely run over.

insights.claim: Perry argues that during COVID, deficits globally of 15-20%, zero rates and Fed corporate credit buying made markets rip despite lockdowns, because liquidity overwhelmed fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Liquidity regimes can trump the economic narrative; model policy flows explicitly.
insights.quote: It turned into a casino because they because they deployed so much liquidity.

insights.claim: When the US Treasury borrows shorter (more bills) in its quarterly refunding it adds liquidity, and when it borrows longer (more coupons) it drains liquidity, making refunding announcements pivotal market dates.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Track the QRA bill/coupon mix as a liquidity signal for risk assets.
insights.quote: If they borrow shorter, there's more liquidity. They borrow longer, there's less liquidity.

insights.claim: On November 1, 2023, Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen shifted issuance from the usual ~80% coupons/20% bills mix toward more short-end borrowing; markets bottomed that day, yields fell and stocks ripped, and Perry says no asset went lower afterward.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: The Nov 2023 QRA is a template for how duration shifts can mark a cross-asset bottom.
insights.quote: I defy any of your listeners to look at November 1, 2023 and see if you can find any asset that went lower. It didn't.

insights.claim: Perry says markets tend to be weak heading into quarterly refunding announcements, an observation drawn from price evidence rather than guesswork.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Consider reducing risk or waiting before QRA dates, then trading the confirmation.
insights.quote: we've found leading into QAS the market tends to be weak

insights.claim: The most recent refunding announcement (around August 5, under Treasury Secretary Bessent) kept duration short and coupon issuance unchanged, which Perry reads as liquidity-supportive, though the market has not yet clearly confirmed it.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Short-duration issuance supports risk, but needs price confirmation before acting.
insights.quote: he kept duration short and when he keeps duration short there's more liquidity

insights.claim: Perry says the five pillars rarely align, and when they do he takes high-conviction positions, citing last year's strong gold call based on tight liquidity, good technicals and favorable seasonality.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Size up only when multiple independent dimensions agree.
insights.quote: Not often do not often do the pillars align.

insights.claim: Perry says looking across liquidity, yield curves and technicals doesn't create bias; when the signals agree it just makes him more confident in the trade, and all of it comes from what the market is showing.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Use agreement across dimensions to set conviction, not to rationalize a view.
insights.quote: It just builds the confidence of the trade to to look across the different dimensions

insights.claim: Perry holds that markets forget major policy dates but prices respect them: no market went a point below the March 20, 2020 low, and the date levels become reference points for re-entry and stops.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Mark policy-event dates on charts as support/resistance and stop locations.
insights.quote: The market doesn't the market forgets it but the dates don't.

insights.claim: Perry flags three current key dates: new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first meeting on June 17, his July 29 meeting, and the August 5 refunding announcement; staying above them makes him more bullish, falling below makes him question the market's strength.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Use these date levels as live bull/bear lines across assets.
insights.quote: If markets are above those dates, it gives me more confidence to be bullish.

insights.claim: Perry treats the annual close as the most important close of the year, judging strength by whether a market trades above last year's close.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Simple regime filter: above or below the prior annual close.
insights.quote: Annual closes.

insights.claim: After the July 29 Fed meeting the market sold off but never closed below that day's level, then rallied hard once softer trimmed mean/PCE data pushed it above; platinum rose about 7% after breaking above the July 29 level.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Holding above an event-date level followed by a break higher is a tradeable confirmation.
insights.quote: platinum went above 28 29th of July went up 7%

insights.claim: Perry is bearish on Bitcoin and Ethereum because Bitcoin can't even reclaim its June 17 level, invoking Paul Tudor Jones's saying 'that dog don't hunt': don't bet on laggards catching up.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Avoid crypto while it lags key date levels; relative weakness signals a reason.
insights.quote: Bitcoin can't even get get above the 17th of June. Forget about the 29th of July. That thing's just a dog.

insights.claim: Perry also counts the recent Bank of Japan/Fed intervention as a key date, along with upcoming nonfarm payrolls (watch wages for inflation) and CPI, because Warsh has said he is data dependent.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Near-term catalysts: NFP wages and CPI determine whether price confirms the date levels.
insights.quote: Chairman Walsh said I'm now data dependent.

themes.theme: QE, the Fed regime and the MOVE index

insights.claim: Perry argues QE1 was essential and prevented a Great Depression-style collapse after the GFC, but QE2 onward, corporate credit buying and 2020 fiscal transfers were 'bad,' worsening inequality and creating inflation.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Distinguish crisis liquidity from serial QE; the latter inflates assets and inflation.
insights.quote: There's no question Q1 was fundamental.

insights.claim: Perry explains that QE adds bank reserves which allow banks to lend more, whereas fiscal policy hands money directly to people, and the 2020 fiscal policies created the inflation.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Fiscal transfers are more directly inflationary than reserve creation.
insights.quote: Fiscal, you get a check from the government.

insights.claim: The new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who resigned from the Fed in 2011 in protest of QE2, wants to return to market price discovery instead of the Fed 'holding everyone's hand,' and markets are struggling to adjust to this regime change.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Expect less Fed backstop and more volatility as policy dogma shifts.
insights.quote: he wants to take us back to price uh finding market as opposed to the Fed holding everyone's hand

insights.claim: Perry suggests the recent market flush and policy moves were coordinated, noting Treasury Secretary Bessent and Fed Chair Warsh both worked for Stanley Druckenmiller.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Treasury-Fed coordination may shape liquidity timing.
insights.quote: Treasury Secretary Bessant and um Chairman Walsh both worked together for Stanley Draen Miller, right?

insights.claim: Perry considers the MOVE index (bond volatility) far more important than the VIX, saying the VIX follows the MOVE, because the financial system runs on Treasury collateral and higher bond vol forces margin increases and de-risking.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Watch bond volatility as the master risk gauge; policymakers prioritize keeping it calm.
insights.quote: The VIX follows the move. The move doesn't follow the VIX.

insights.claim: Perry's models use year-over-year rate of change because banks and hedge funds run VaR models with roughly a one-year lookback; with the MOVE around 78 now versus a similar level a year ago (and about 120 in March, ~180 in 2023), comparisons are tough and VaR-driven risk capacity remains relatively tight.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Year-over-year vol comps drive institutional risk budgets; a flat MOVE means little VaR expansion.
insights.quote: we compare a rate of change on a yearly basis

insights.claim: Perry recommends volatility-adjusting all positions: trade far smaller in KOSPI (implied vol near 100 recently) than in the S&P 500 (~16% vol).
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Scale size inversely to volatility to keep risk and emotions manageable.
insights.quote: ultimately you got to you got to volatility adjust your risk

themes.theme: Recent trades and current market view

insights.claim: Perry's pillars drove a profitable short in South Korea's KOSPI and Taiwan, on the view that the Middle East crisis hurt food- and energy-dependent Asian economies while the world was 'over its skis' on AI; KOSPI then sold off about 40%.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Energy-importing, AI-heavy Asian markets are vulnerable to Middle East shocks.
insights.quote: the world was over their skis on AI and you had that 40% sell off in Cosby

insights.claim: Instead of buying oil during the Middle East crisis, Perry went long corn, wheat and soy because oil volatility was ~70% and much phosphate comes from the Middle East, using ratio trades (long strongest, short weakest).
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Second-order expression: fertilizer supply shocks favor agriculture over crowded, volatile oil.
insights.quote: So, we were very long corn, wheat, and soy as the crisis occurred.

insights.claim: Perry names the Middle East as the dominant Pillar One (geopolitical) factor at the moment.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Geopolitics is the current top driver in his framework.
insights.quote: pillar one at the moment to me is probably probably the main one is the Middle East

insights.claim: Perry sees 'crashes within the crash': a ~45% selloff in Asia, crypto falling from 120 to 50, silver from 100 to 50, while the S&P 500 makes new highs; he has not called a top.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Leverage-driven pockets can collapse while indexes hold up; dispersion is high.
insights.quote: at the moment, you are seeing crashes within the crash, but at the same time, you're also seeing the S&P 500 and new highs

insights.claim: Perry attributes South Korea's crash to high margin debt as young traders piled into AI names believing they couldn't fall.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Margin-debt build-ups in retail-heavy markets are a crash precursor.
insights.quote: the the margin debt to ratio was the reason why it crashed

insights.claim: Perry describes current markets as choppy with crosswinds: Trump tantrums, the Middle East, a dogma-changing new Fed chair, and uncertainty about whether AI capex is a productivity miracle or overspending.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Lower-conviction environment; keep size modest and trade what is in front of you.
insights.quote: everyone's trying to work out is a productivity miracle. Are they spending too much money?

insights.claim: Perry is a fan of gold because the monetary system has become vulnerable through all the policy tinkering since 2008.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Structural case for gold as a hedge against policy-distorted monetary system.
insights.quote: I'm a big fan of gold because the monetary system is vulnerable

insights.claim: Perry argues crypto's 2020-21 rally (including memecoins like Fartcoin reaching ~$2B market caps) was purely a liquidity effect, not adoption as a payment system, which is why most holders lost their gains once liquidity dried up.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: If you don't know why you made money you won't keep it; crypto is a liquidity beta.
insights.quote: The reason it went up is because liquidity went through the roof and everything went up.

insights.claim: Perry says top traders win only about 55-57% of the time; the edge comes from cutting losses quickly and letting winners run larger, and anyone claiming 80-90% win rates is lying.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Optimize payoff asymmetry, not hit rate.
insights.quote: the good ones run around 55 [clears throat] to 57

insights.claim: Perry uses a 1-5 risk-unit scale: 3-5 units when he is 'seeing it' and 1 unit when he isn't; uniform small sizing regardless of conviction won't make money.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Vary size with conviction to make the 57% win rate pay.
insights.quote: When you're seeing it, you got to you got to three to five units.

insights.claim: Perry insists on always trading with hard stop losses, calling inability to take losses the biggest mistake of retail and learning traders.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Non-negotiable: every position has a stop.
insights.quote: Never ever not have a stop loss.

insights.claim: Perry says risk/reward must match the time frame: buying the S&P at 7,000 targeting 10,000 with a 10-point stop is nonsense; long-term targets need long-term thinking and wider risk.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Align stops, targets and holding period.
insights.quote: There's no point looking for longer long longerterm moves with shorter term thinking.

insights.claim: At Tudor, new PMs got about $50 million with a 10% drawdown limit and a two-year contract; hitting the drawdown meant automatic termination, and failing to deploy capital could also cost your job. One colleague grew from $50 million to over $1.5 billion in ten years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Institutional benchmark: hard drawdown limits plus a mandate to use risk.
insights.quote: they gave us like $50 million of capital at the start with a 10% draw down

insights.claim: When hiring, Tudor examined a candidate's daily return data, specifically the worst day and how they performed after it, rejecting those who 'go into their shell' in drawdown.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Evaluate your own post-drawdown behavior as a key edge metric.
insights.quote: they go to that, you know, your your returns and look at your worst day. Then they'll see how you behave after that

insights.claim: Perry warns that more capital is often allocated right after a good run, which is the worst timing, and that managing $500M-$1B+ is far harder because liquidity becomes a constraint.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Beware scaling up after hot streaks; size capacity shrinks with liquidity.
insights.quote: you get allocated more capital just after you've had a good run

insights.claim: Perry, who has watched four major crises (Nasdaq bust, GFC, 2012 Europe, 2020), says leverage without risk management is what got people 'body bagged' each time.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Leverage is the common killer across cycles.
insights.quote: I've seen four major events and I've seen people body bagged through all those events

insights.claim: For long-only investors, Perry's hedge is simply to de-risk into cash; as a trader he avoids 'hedging' and actively trades volatility instead, while avoiding silly volatility like KOSPI swinging ±20% on consecutive days.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Cash is the hedge for passive money; actively manage for traders.
insights.quote: we just tell people to take, you know, d-risisk their markets and put more money into cash

insights.claim: Paul Tudor Jones removed capital from any PM going through separation or divorce for three months, and Tudor provided psychologist coaches focused on emotional construct rather than trading.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Life stress degrades decisions; cut risk during personal turmoil.
insights.quote: if any of his PMs were going through a separation or a divorce he'd take the capital off them for 3 months

insights.claim: Perry says the year you enter markets shapes your bias: starting in 2011 makes you bullish, starting in 1987 (his first year) makes you bearish, and macro traders must constantly confront it; he notes 1987 still closed the year higher.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Audit your structural directional bias.
insights.quote: if you entered the market in 1987, like I did, you definitely have a bias of being bearish

insights.claim: Paul Tudor Jones's key skill is changing his mind quickly, flipping from long to short; his public 'bullish Bitcoin' remarks can be reversed the same afternoon, so followers shouldn't copy TV calls.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Don't treat famous traders' media comments as durable positions.
insights.quote: he's exceptional at changing his mind. He can go from long to short like that.

insights.claim: Perry contrasts Paul Tudor Jones (nimble, more of a portfolio) with Stanley Druckenmiller (concentrated, straps on big risk when right), saying traders should choose a style compatible with their emotional construct.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Match strategy to temperament.
insights.quote: Jones is in awe of of of Stan Lee Draen Miller's uh ability to to to strap on risk where Paul's much more nimble.

insights.claim: Perry argues one-dimensional pure technicians should become systematic quant traders instead, because he has never seen a successful discretionary trader who ignores yield curves and liquidity.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Discretionary traders need multi-dimensional inputs; pure TA belongs in systems.
insights.quote: if you're just a technician, I I'd argue you're better off trying to build [clears throat] out a quantitative model

insights.claim: Perry says serious global macro trading requires following all 15 weekly sessions (Asia, Europe, US) and the handoffs between them, and keeping a daily journal reviewed each morning and weekend.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Session transfers carry information; journaling compounds learning.
insights.quote: Your journal must be your gospel.

insights.claim: Perry, now 58, says he ranked only around the top 50% at Tudor and is a much stronger trader today, stressing patience: 'there's always another train at the station,' citing the 2012-13 Abenomics trade when USD/JPY went from 80 to 115 and the Nikkei doubled.
insights.speaker: Andrew Perry
insights.so_what: Big regime trades come periodically; survive the tough stretches to be there.
insights.quote: Dolly went from 80 to 115 in like 6 weeks.
